vignette:
The Weight of What He Knows

Marcus is twenty-six years old, a detective with the city's crimes-against-persons unit, and he spends his days building cases against people who hurt the ones they claim to love. The irony is not lost on him. He has learned to live inside that irony the way you learn to live inside a house with a broken furnace — you stop noticing the cold until someone else mentions it.

The relationship with Darian lasted fourteen months. It began the way Marcus describes most good things in his life: fast, certain, electric. Darian was older, confident, and Marcus, who had grown up being told he was too sensitive for police work, found something that felt like steadiness in that confidence. The first time Darian shoved him into a doorframe, Marcus told himself it was stress. The second time, a closed fist against his jaw, he told himself he had provoked it. By the time the episodes became regular — objects thrown, hands around his throat, a broken wrist explained to his supervisor as a training accident — Marcus had constructed an entire internal architecture of justification. He was a detective. He knew what abuse looked like. Therefore, what was happening to him could not be abuse.

He left after an incident eighteen months ago that he still cannot describe in full. He will say only that he drove himself to the emergency room and that the attending nurse asked him twice if he was safe at home. He said yes both times. He went back to the apartment, packed a bag, and never returned. Three months later, he married his longtime partner, Renee, a woman he describes as the most patient person alive. He believes this. He also believes, in the part of himself he cannot quiet, that she will eventually see through him to whatever it was that made him deserve what happened.

Sleep is where Marcus loses the most ground. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart already running, certain that someone is in the room. He lies still, listening, running threat assessments the way he was trained to, and the absurdity of this — a trained detective conducting tactical evaluations of his own bedroom — fills him with a shame he cannot name. He does not tell Renee why he is awake. He goes to the kitchen and sits at the table until the feeling passes.

At work, he is considered one of the best interviewers in the unit. He is particularly skilled with male victims of domestic violence, who are often reluctant to speak. His colleagues attribute this to instinct. Marcus knows it is something else. He knows exactly how a person sounds when they are minimizing. He knows the specific grammar of self-blame. When he sits across from a man who has been hurt by someone who loved him, Marcus feels something open in his chest — not compassion exactly, but recognition, which is its own kind of unbearable.

He startles at raised voices in the precinct. He has developed a habit of positioning himself near exits in restaurants, which Renee has noticed and which he has explained as occupational habit. Technically, this is true. He avoids the neighborhood where he and Darian lived, rerouting his commute by eleven minutes every day without consciously deciding to do so. When a case brings him into contact with a male perpetrator who resembles Darian in build or manner, he feels his hands go cold and his thinking narrow in a way that frightens him.

What Marcus finds hardest to explain, even to himself, is the grief. He is not grieving Darian. He understands, professionally and intellectually, exactly what Darian was. What he grieves is the version of himself that existed before — the one who did not check the locks three times, who did not flinch at the sound of keys in a door, who did not lie awake conducting threat assessments of his own bedroom, in his own home, next to the woman who loves him.

He wants that person back. He is not sure that person still exists.
